title: Ezekiel 30:20–26
context: Ezekiel 30:20–26 is dated to the eleventh year, first month, seventh day, often placed in spring 587 BC. The LORD tells the prophet that he has broken the arm of Pharaoh and that it has not been bound up so that it can hold a sword. He will break both of Pharaoh’s arms, scatter the Egyptians, and strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, putting his own sword in that king’s hand. Many connect the broken arm with Egypt’s failed attempt to relieve the siege of Jerusalem described in Jeremiah 37:5–11, though Ezekiel does not say so directly. Both traditions read the unit as the LORD’s sovereign rule over the strength of kings, and as a warning to Judah not to rely on Egypt.

verses.text: In the eleventh year, in the first month, in the seventh day of the month, the LORD’s word came to me, saying,
verses.arminianNotes: The prophet reports a word dated to the eleventh year, first month, seventh day. Arminian readers see this oracle given during the siege of Jerusalem, when Judah still hoped for help from Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the date as connecting the oracle with the crisis of the siege. Both traditions hold the modern date loosely, often placing it in spring 587 BC.

verses.text: “Son of man, I have broken the arm of Pharaoh king of Egypt. Behold, it has not been bound up, to apply medicines, to put a bandage to bind it, that it may become strong to hold the sword.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he has broken Pharaoh’s arm, and it has not been bandaged to grow strong enough to hold a sword. Arminians see God’s judgment already at work, weakening Egypt’s military power.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereignty in limiting Pharaoh’s strength. Both traditions note that many connect this with Egypt’s failed attempt to relieve Jerusalem (Jeremiah 37:5–11), though Ezekiel does not say so directly.

verses.text: Therefore the Lord GOD says: ‘Behold, I am against Pharaoh king of Egypt, and will break his arms, the strong arm, and that which was broken. I will cause the sword to fall out of his hand.
verses.arminianNotes: The Lord GOD says he is against Pharaoh and will break both his arms, the strong and the broken, so the sword falls from his hand. Arminian readers see the completion of Egypt’s weakening, leaving it unable to fight.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s power to remove all human strength. Both traditions read the image as poetic, describing Egypt’s complete military collapse.

verses.text: I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations, and will disperse them through the countries.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the countries. Arminians see the same judgment that Judah faced, now applied to Egypt.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and read the verse as repeating 29:12. Both traditions see the repetition as reinforcing the certainty of the judgment.

verses.text: I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon, and put my sword in his hand; but I will break the arms of Pharaoh, and he will groan before the king of Babylon with the groaning of a mortally wounded man.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put his sword in his hand, but break Pharaoh’s arms. Arminian readers see God directing history, giving strength to one king and taking it from another.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s sovereign rule over the strength of nations. Both traditions note that how God uses Babylon is discussed at the Judges 9:23 box.

verses.text: I will hold up the arms of the king of Babylon, but the arms of Pharaoh will fall down. Then they will know that I am the LORD when I put my sword into the hand of the king of Babylon, and he stretches it out on the land of Egypt.
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will hold up Babylon’s arms while Pharaoh’s fall, and they will know he is the LORD when he puts his sword in Babylon’s hand. Arminians see the contrast between the two kings as showing that power comes from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see God’s glory revealed in the outcome. Both traditions hold the recognition formula as shared ground and read the verse as a warning against trusting Egypt.

verses.text: I will scatter the Egyptians among the nations and disperse them through the countries. Then they will know that I am the LORD.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: The LORD says he will scatter the Egyptians, and they will know he is the LORD. Arminian readers see the unit closing with the same refrain, which ties judgment to recognition of God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers agree and see the repetition as emphasizing God’s purpose. Both traditions read the verse as completing the oracle of the broken arms.
